A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DFT/DFT2 research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–B support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original DFT/DFT2 experiments on mathematical reasoning and general-language benchmarks, along with moving-average, negative-sample-count, and prompting analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds comparator experiments, training curves, additional model evaluations, and sampling-temperature results.

M1.justification: The DFT and DFT2 objectives, sampling procedures, moving-average updates, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged. Appendix A.1 newly specifies which existing scoring function each variant uses; it does not introduce a different method.

E1.justification: The MetaMathQA, UltraFeedback, and UltraChat training coverage and existing math, general-language, and instruction-following evaluations are retained. The additional Qwen and Llama experiments reuse UltraFeedback and the same seven benchmarks, extending model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated ORPO and DPO-p baselines. Table 1 removes RFT-7B, Qwen-7B, Mistral-7B-base with eight shots, WizardMath-7B, and Llama-2-70B, retaining the MetaMath comparators. These are limited membership changes within the established comparison families.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the experimental design with Qwen-2.5-0.5B and Llama3-8B-instruct configurations, a two-stage SFT→PO control using the same generated negatives as DFT, and sampling temperatures of 0, 0.3, 0.7, and 1.0. Efficiency evaluation changes from seconds per iteration to total training hours. Existing benchmark settings are newly documented rather than demonstrably changed.

E4.justification: New Figure 3 examines positive and negative likelihood trajectories for DFT, SFT, and SimPO. New Table 4 tests single-stage versus two-stage training with matched generated negatives, while Appendix B.6 tests sensitivity to sampling temperature. These materially expand the analyses beyond the retained moving-average, sample-count, and prompting studies.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional results retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: Original DFT/DFT2 math and Mistral/UltraFeedback scores remain unchanged, but substantial results are added. Table 4 reports averages of 58.57 and 56.98 for SFT→DPO and SFT→SimPO using generated negatives, versus 62.84 and 62.56 for DFT and DFT2. Tables 10–12 add model and temperature results. Comparator rows and likelihood curves are added, five math-baseline rows are removed, and total-hour measurements replace per-iteration timing results.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, derivations, and Equations 1–14 are retained. The added comparison with finite-label classification and identification of the objective as empirical X-risk minimization explain and position existing mathematics; they add no formal result or proof.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, and introduction qualify the broad avoidance of preference data to human preference data and describe mitigating collection or reward-model-training burdens rather than eliminating them. DFT is presented as an improved SFT variant, while the principal framework, optimization, and comparative-performance claims remain. The conclusion retains the earlier broader wording.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new likelihood curves as showing that DFT preserves positive-example likelihood while suppressing generated negatives, unlike SimPO's declining positive likelihood. It also interprets the matched-negative comparison as favoring single-stage training and describes DFT2's total training efficiency as comparable to SFT→DPO. Earlier length-bias and overfitting interpretations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds explicit scoring-function choices and benchmark-specific shots, metrics, and chat-template usage. It also discloses four A100 80GB GPUs, timing boundaries, and approximately 1.33 hours of excluded negative-generation time. The listed code location changes from PenGuln/DFT to Optimization-AI/DFT. Existing detailed training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds ORPO, DPO-positive, and X-risk references, removes the Radford and Wu references, and corrects SPIN's attribution to the already cited Chen et al. work. Section 4 more explicitly connects DFT to discriminative representation learning and X-risk optimization, without broadly restructuring its research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, introductory framing and terminology are refined, and explanatory paragraphs and appendix subsections are added. Author, affiliation, acknowledgment, and publication-header text also changes. The main section order and most methodological and experimental prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with likelihood-curve panels and tables for matched-negative comparisons, benchmark settings, additional models, and sampling temperatures. The timing chart is redrawn with total-hour axes and separate training-phase colors. Tables 1–2 are shortened or expanded, comparison captions are clarified, and main-result displays are rearranged; existing analysis plots are retained under new numbering.

improvement.justification: The matched-negative two-stage comparison and additional model tests strengthen evidence that previously relied on DFT experiments using Mistral alone. Explicit evaluation settings and more informative timing disclosure also improve reproducibility and efficiency assessment. However, Observation 2 still says self-play PO cannot improve SFT even though the new ORPO row averages 61.97 versus SFT's 61.79, and uncertainty reporting remains absent. The net improvement is useful but limited.
